entries.label: prepositional phrase
entries.meaning: Wanted or needed by many people, often more than the available supply.
entries.usage: Common in business news, job ads and conversation about skills, products and services. Patterns are *be in high demand* and *in high demand among / with* + group. *In great demand* is also correct, and *in such high demand* is common for emphasis.
entries.pattern: be in high demand (among + group)
examples: Electricians are **in high demand**, so my nephew had three job offers before he finished his training.
Tickets for the reunion tour were **in such high demand** that they sold out in minutes.
Small apartments near the university are always **in high demand** in August.

drill.sentence: Good babysitters are {{in high demand}} in our neighborhood, so book early for New Year's Eve.
drill.hint: wanted by a lot of people (the adjective is not *great*)

mistake.wrong: Nurses are highly demanded in this area.
mistake.right: Nurses are in high demand in this area.
mistake.why: Natives describe this with the phrase *in high demand*; the passive *highly demanded* sounds like a translation.

entries.related: *in demand* — same idea, a bit weaker; *sought-after* — an adjective that sounds more elegant; *in short supply* — hard to get because there is too little.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To decide on something specific that you want to achieve, often by a certain time.
entries.usage: Common in sports, business, education and self-improvement talk. Typical patterns are *set a goal of* + noun or *-ing*, *set a goal to* + verb and *set yourself a goal*, often with *realistic, ambitious* or *clear*. Once it is set, you *reach*, *achieve* or *meet* a goal.
entries.pattern: set (yourself) a goal of + noun / -ing; set a goal to + verb
examples: This year I **set a goal** of reading one book a month, and so far I'm ahead.
The company has **set a goal** to cut its energy use in half by 2030.
Our coach told us to **set realistic goals** instead of promising to win every race.

drill.sentence: When I started running, I {{set a goal}} of finishing a 5K without stopping.
drill.hint: decided on something to aim for (the noun is not *target*)

entries.related: *set a target* — similar, often with numbers at work; *aim for* — try to reach; *achieve / reach a goal* — succeed.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To be as good as people expected or hoped.
entries.usage: Common in business, reviews, performance reports and sports. Typical patterns are *meet (someone's) expectations*, *fail to meet expectations* and *exceed expectations* (be better than expected). *Live up to expectations* means the same and is a bit more conversational.
entries.pattern: meet / exceed / fail to meet (someone's) expectations
examples: The hotel was nice, but it didn't **meet our expectations** for the price.
The company said holiday sales had **met expectations**, and its stock rose slightly.
Her performance review says she **meets expectations**, which she found a little disappointing.

drill.sentence: The sequel was fun, but after such a great first movie, it didn't quite {{meet our expectations}}.
drill.hint: be as good as we'd hoped (not *live up to*)

entries.related: *live up to expectations* — same, more conversational; *exceed expectations* — be better than expected; *fall short of expectations* — be worse than expected.

entries.label: prepositional phrase
entries.meaning: Although most people believe the opposite; it introduces a fact that corrects a common belief.
entries.usage: Common in journalism, popular science, teaching and conversation, usually at the start of a sentence and followed by a comma. Used on its own, it has no article; *the* appears only before a *that* clause (*contrary to the popular belief that …*). It can sound like a cliché in essays.
entries.pattern: Contrary to popular belief, + clause
examples: **Contrary to popular belief**, most small businesses don't fail in their first year.
Bulls, **contrary to popular belief**, aren't angered by the color red; they react to the movement of the cape.
Seattle actually gets less rain each year than New York, **contrary to popular belief**.

drill.sentence: {{Contrary to popular belief}}, cracking your knuckles doesn't cause arthritis.
drill.hint: although most people think otherwise (the adjective is not *common*)

mistake.wrong: Contrary to the popular belief, camels don't store water in their humps.
mistake.right: Contrary to popular belief, camels don't store water in their humps.
mistake.why: Used alone, the phrase has no article; *the* is only used before a *that* clause.

entries.related: *contrary to what many people think* — plainer; *a common misconception* — the wrong belief itself; *believe it or not* — casual, introduces a surprising fact.

entries.label: adverb + adjective
entries.meaning: Completely sensible and fair; not at all unreasonable.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, emails and negotiations, often to defend a request or to reassure someone: *That's a perfectly reasonable question.* *Perfectly* here means "completely", as in *perfectly fine* or *perfectly normal*. It can sound slightly defensive: *I had a perfectly reasonable explanation!*
entries.pattern: a perfectly reasonable + request / question / explanation; it's perfectly reasonable to + verb
examples: Asking for a refund when the gym was closed for half the month is **perfectly reasonable**.
It's **perfectly reasonable** to want some time alone after a long day with the kids.
My boss turned down what seemed like a **perfectly reasonable** request to work from home on Fridays.

drill.sentence: Don't apologize for asking; it's a {{perfectly reasonable}} question, and lots of people wonder the same thing.
drill.hint: entirely sensible (the adverb is not *completely* or *totally*)

entries.related: *fair enough* — casual, accepts someone's point; *understandable* — easy to accept emotionally; *unreasonable* — the opposite.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To follow or record something carefully so that you always know its current state or where it is.
entries.usage: Very common in speech and writing about money, time, health, tasks and people. The pattern is *keep track of* + noun or a *wh-* clause (*keep track of how much you spend*). The opposite is *lose track of*, as in *I lost track of time*.
entries.pattern: keep track of + noun / how much / where …; lose track of
examples: I use a simple spreadsheet to **keep track of** what we spend on groceries each month.
With four kids in different sports, it's hard to **keep track of** who needs to be where.
The app helps patients **keep track of** their blood sugar during the day.

drill.sentence: My dad writes everything on the calendar on the fridge so he can {{keep track of}} everyone's appointments.
drill.hint: follow carefully so he always knows (verb + noun + *of*)

entries.related: *lose track of* — the opposite; *keep tabs on* — informal, watch someone or something closely; *stay on top of* — keep control of a lot of tasks.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: An essential part of something, without which it would not be complete or work properly.
entries.usage: Common in formal speech, business, education and official writing; in conversation people more often say *a big part* or *a key part*. The pattern is *an integral part of* + noun, often after *be*, *become* or *form*. It is stronger than *an important part*: without it, the whole would not work.
entries.pattern: be / become / form an integral part of + noun
examples: Music is **an integral part of** every family gathering at my grandparents' house.
Clinical rotations are **an integral part of** nursing school, not an optional extra.
Over the years, the old train station has become **an integral part of** the town's identity.

drill.sentence: For most Americans, the car is {{an integral part of}} daily life, especially outside big cities.
drill.hint: a piece it couldn't do without (a formal adjective; not *essential*, *important* or *key*)

entries.related: *a key part* — important, more conversational; *an essential part* — very close in meaning; *part and parcel of* — idiomatic, a natural part of something, often an unpleasant one.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To make something bad less likely to happen.
entries.usage: Very common in health advice, safety instructions, finance and news. The pattern is *reduce the risk of* + noun or *-ing*, often with *greatly* or *significantly*; *lower* and *cut* are close alternatives. In health writing, *reduce your risk of* + illness is the standard phrase.
entries.pattern: reduce the / your risk of + noun / -ing
examples: Washing your hands before you eat can **reduce the risk of** getting sick.
Smoke alarms on every floor greatly **reduce the risk of** dying in a house fire.
Spreading your money across different funds **reduces the risk of** losing everything at once.

drill.sentence: Wearing a helmet {{reduces the risk of}} serious head injuries when you ride a bike.
drill.hint: makes something bad less likely (the verb is not *lowers* or *cuts*)

mistake.wrong: Exercise reduces the risk to get heart disease.
mistake.right: Exercise reduces the risk of getting heart disease.
mistake.why: *Risk* is followed by *of* + noun or *-ing*, not by *to* + verb.

entries.related: *lower the risk* — same, slightly more casual; *minimize the risk* — reduce it as much as possible; *increase / raise the risk* — the opposite.

entries.label: prepositional phrase
entries.meaning: As the representative of someone, or instead of them, so that you speak or act for them.
entries.usage: Common in speeches, emails, business and law. Both *on behalf of* + noun and *on someone's behalf* are normal (*I'm calling on my mother's behalf*). A frequent formula in speeches is *On behalf of* + group, *I'd like to thank …*.
entries.pattern: on behalf of + person / group; on someone's behalf
examples: **On behalf of** everyone at the store, thank you for twenty years of service.
My lawyer will speak **on my behalf**, so I don't have to say anything.
She accepted the award **on behalf of** her late father, who had started the charity.

drill.sentence: My mom doesn't speak much English, so I talk to her doctors {{on her behalf}}.
drill.hint: as her representative (not *for her*)

mistake.wrong: I'm writing in the name of my company.
mistake.right: I'm writing on behalf of my company.
mistake.why: To act as someone's representative, English uses *on behalf of*; *in the name of* is for authority or causes (*in the name of the law*).

entries.related: *for* — the plain word; *in someone's place* — instead of them; *represent* — the verb.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To use a chance, offer or situation to get a benefit from it.
entries.usage: Very common in speech, ads and advice: *Take advantage of our summer sale.* With things and chances, it is positive or neutral. With people (*take advantage of someone*), it is negative: it means to exploit or unfairly use them.
entries.pattern: take (full) advantage of + chance / offer / situation
examples: We **took advantage of** the warm weekend to paint the fence.
If your employer matches your retirement savings, **take full advantage of** it.
Thousands of shoppers **took advantage of** the free shipping on Black Friday.

drill.sentence: While the kids were at camp, we {{took advantage of}} the quiet house and finally cleaned out the garage.
drill.hint: used the chance offered by (not *made the most of*)

entries.related: *make the most of* — use as well as possible; *seize the opportunity* — act quickly on a chance; *exploit* — use unfairly, negative.

entries.label: adverb + adjective
entries.meaning: Easy to get, find or buy whenever you need it.
entries.usage: Common in news, product information and health writing; it sounds a bit more formal than *easy to find*. It usually follows *be* or *become*, often with *to* + people (*readily available to students*). *Freely available* is different: it means available without cost or restrictions.
entries.pattern: be / become readily available (to + people / in + places)
examples: Fresh tortillas are **readily available** in almost every grocery store in Texas.
In the early 1990s, cell phones weren't nearly as **readily available** as they are today.
Help is **readily available**; the crisis hotline is open twenty-four hours a day.

drill.sentence: Clean drinking water isn't {{readily available}} in some rural areas, so families have to buy it in bottles.
drill.hint: easy to get (the adverb is not *easily* or *widely*)

entries.related: *widely available* — sold or found in many places; *at hand* — near and ready to use; *hard to come by* — the opposite.

entries.label: noun phrase
entries.meaning: Care to get every small part of a task exactly right.
entries.usage: Very common in job ads, references, reviews and praise of craftsmanship: *excellent attention to detail*. It takes no article, and *detail* stays singular. Typical verbs are *require, show* and *have*, and typical adjectives are *great, careful* and *meticulous*.
entries.pattern: (great / careful) attention to detail; require / show attention to detail
examples: The job ad asks for strong communication skills and **attention to detail**.
You can see the chef's **attention to detail** in every plate, down to the tiny edible flowers.
Restoring old furniture takes patience and real **attention to detail**.

drill.sentence: The painter was slow, but his {{attention to detail}} meant there wasn't a single drip on the floor.
drill.hint: care about every small thing (not an *eye for* …)

mistake.wrong: Strong attention to details is required.
mistake.right: Strong attention to detail is required.
mistake.why: In this fixed phrase, *detail* is singular and uncountable.

entries.related: *an eye for detail* — a natural ability to notice small things; *meticulous* — extremely careful about details; *sloppy* — careless, the opposite.

entries.label: verb phrase
entries.meaning: To use a chance, time or situation as well as you can, so that you get as much benefit as possible from it.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation and advice, often about limited time or good conditions: *Let's make the most of the sunshine.* The pattern is *make the most of* + noun. It also works for bad situations: *We made the most of a rainy vacation* means you still enjoyed it as much as possible.
entries.pattern: make the most of + chance / time / situation
examples: We only have two days in Rome, so let's **make the most of** them.
He's **making the most of** his retirement: golf twice a week and a trip every spring.
The power was out all evening, so we **made the most of** it with candles and board games.

drill.sentence: Summer is short here, so we try to {{make the most of}} every sunny weekend.
drill.hint: get as much as possible out of (not *take advantage of*)

entries.related: *make the best of* — accept a bad situation and do what you can; *take advantage of* — use a chance for benefit; *seize the day* — enjoy the present.

entries.label: prepositional phrase
entries.meaning: Being managed successfully, so that there is no danger, chaos or further growth of a problem.
entries.usage: Very common in speech and news: *Everything's under control.* Patterns are *get / bring / keep something under control* and *be under control*; typical subjects are fires, costs, symptoms, emotions and children. The opposite is *out of control*.
entries.pattern: get / keep / bring + noun + under control; be under control
examples: Firefighters finally got the blaze **under control** after twelve hours.
With the right medication, her asthma is now **under control**.
"Do you need help in the kitchen?" "No thanks, everything's **under control**."

drill.sentence: We need to get our spending {{under control}} before we can think about buying a house.
drill.hint: managed so it stops growing (not *in check*)

entries.related: *in check* — kept from getting worse; *in hand* — being dealt with; *out of control* — the opposite.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To make people notice something, often a problem or a fact they had ignored.
entries.usage: Common in news, campaigns, speeches and conversation. The pattern is *draw attention to* + noun; *draw attention away from* means to distract people from something. *Draw attention to yourself* is often negative: to make others look at you.
entries.pattern: draw attention to + noun; draw attention away from + noun
examples: The students organized a walkout to **draw attention to** the lack of school counselors.
I tried to cover the stain on my shirt without **drawing attention to** it.
The report **draws attention to** how few parks there are in low-income neighborhoods.

drill.sentence: The museum hung a huge banner outside to {{draw attention to}} its new dinosaur exhibit.
drill.hint: make people notice (the verb is not *call*, *bring* or *attract*)

entries.related: *call attention to* — same, a bit more formal; *highlight* — emphasize a point; *attract attention* — make people look, often without a specific target.

entries.label: noun phrase
entries.meaning: The amount of money people need to pay for basic things such as housing, food, transportation and health care.
entries.usage: Common in news, economics, salary negotiations and conversation about moving. Typical patterns are *a high / low cost of living*, *the rising cost of living* and *the cost of living in* + place. A *cost-of-living raise* or *adjustment* is a pay increase that matches rising prices.
entries.pattern: the (rising) cost of living (in + place); a cost-of-living raise
examples: We moved from San Francisco to Pittsburgh because **the cost of living** is so much lower.
Many workers are asking for raises to keep up with **the cost of living**.
Retirees on a fixed income feel every increase in **the cost of living**.

drill.sentence: Salaries are higher in New York, but so is {{the cost of living}}, so you may not end up with more money.
drill.hint: what it takes to pay for basics like rent and food (a four-word noun phrase)

mistake.wrong: The cost of life in Zurich is very high.
mistake.right: The cost of living in Zurich is very high.
mistake.why: English uses the *-ing* form here: *the cost of living*.

entries.related: *living expenses* — the money a person spends on basics; *inflation* — the general rise in prices; *affordability* — how easy something is to pay for.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To make people doubt something or wonder whether it is true, right or safe.
entries.usage: Common in news, reports and serious discussion. The subject is often an event, a fact or a finding (*The delays raise questions about the contractor*), but people can raise questions too. Patterns are *raise (serious) questions about* + noun and *raise the question of whether* + clause.
entries.pattern: raise (serious) questions about + noun; raise the question of whether …
examples: The head coach's sudden resignation has **raised questions about** the team's future.
The unlocked back door **raises questions about** who was in the house that night.
A new study **raises questions about** whether vitamin supplements do any good.

drill.sentence: The seller's refusal to let us see the car in person {{raises questions about}} whether it's really in good shape.
drill.hint: make people wonder (verb + plural noun + preposition; the noun is not *doubts*)

entries.related: *cast doubt on* — make something seem less certain, more formal; *call into question* — openly challenge; *ask questions* — directly question someone.

entries.label: prepositional phrase
entries.meaning: Impossible to manage, stop or limit, and often getting worse quickly.
entries.usage: Very common in speech and news about fires, prices, vehicles, parties, children and emotions. Patterns are *be / get / spin out of control*; *spiral out of control* stresses fast worsening. Before a noun it is hyphenated: *an out-of-control truck*.
entries.pattern: be / get / spin / spiral out of control; an out-of-control + noun
examples: The truck's brakes failed, and it rolled **out of control** down the hill.
My credit card debt was **out of control** until a counselor helped me make a plan.
A small party at a neighbor's house spiraled **out of control** when someone posted the address online.

drill.sentence: The fire spread so fast through the dry hills that it was soon {{out of control}}.
drill.hint: impossible to manage or stop (a prepositional phrase; not *out of hand*)

entries.related: *under control* — the opposite; *get out of hand* — informal, similar; *spiral out of control* — get worse faster and faster.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To do careful, systematic research on a subject, usually in a formal or professional setting.
entries.usage: Formal; typical of academic writing, reports, funding applications and job ads. The patterns are *conduct research on / into* + topic; in conversation people usually say *do research*. *Research* is uncountable, so for one unit use *a study* or *a research project*.
entries.pattern: conduct research on / into + topic
examples: Before opening the café, she **conducted** market **research** to find out what the neighborhood wanted.
Scientists at the station **conduct research** on how melting ice affects ocean currents.
The children's hospital **conducts research** into new treatments for rare diseases.

drill.sentence: The company hired an outside firm to {{conduct research}} into why customers were canceling their subscriptions.
drill.hint: formally investigate (the verb is not *do* or *carry out*)

mistake.wrong: We conducted a research on sleep habits.
mistake.right: We conducted research on sleep habits.
mistake.why: *Research* is uncountable, so it takes no *a*; say *a study* or *a research project* for one unit.

entries.related: *do research* — the everyday form; *carry out research* — also formal; *a study* — one countable piece of research.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: A way of solving a problem that will keep working for years, not just for a short time.
entries.usage: Common in news, business and practical advice, often in contrast with a temporary fix: *This is not a long-term solution.* Typical verbs are *find*, *need* and *offer*; *a solution to* + problem is the standard form. *Long-term* has a hyphen before a noun.
entries.pattern: find / need a long-term solution to + problem
examples: Buckets under the leak are fine for tonight, but we need **a long-term solution**.
The city is looking for **a long-term solution** to the shortage of affordable housing.
Painkillers helped my back, but my doctor says physical therapy is **a better long-term solution**.

drill.sentence: Moving the kids into one bedroom works for now, but it's not {{a long-term solution}}.
drill.hint: a fix that will work for years (the adjective is not *permanent*)

entries.related: *a quick fix* — the opposite, fast but temporary; *a stopgap* — a temporary measure until a real solution is found; *a permanent solution* — one that ends the problem.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To reduce the amount of money that a business, organization or person spends.
entries.usage: Very common in business news and in everyday talk about money. The usual pattern is *cut costs by* + *-ing*; *cost-cutting* is the noun or adjective (*cost-cutting measures*). Said about companies, it often hints at job losses or lower quality.
entries.pattern: cut costs (by + -ing); cost-cutting measures
examples: The airline **cut costs** by charging for snacks and checked bags.
We're trying to **cut costs** at home by cooking more and eating out less.
To **cut costs**, the rural school district switched to a four-day week.

drill.sentence: The restaurant {{cut costs}} by switching to a cheaper energy supplier and closing on Mondays.
drill.hint: spent less (verb + noun; not *saved money*)

entries.related: *cut back on* — spend less on something specific; *cut corners* — save money or time by doing a worse job; *tighten your belt* — informal, spend less.

entries.label: adverb + adjective
entries.meaning: Strongly connected, or very similar because of a shared origin or cause.
entries.usage: Common in science, news and everyday talk about families, languages, species and problems. The patterns are *closely related to* + noun and *A and B are closely related*. For family, *distantly related* is the opposite.
entries.pattern: A is closely related to B; A and B are closely related
examples: Wolves and dogs are so **closely related** that they can have puppies together.
Doctors say anxiety and depression are **closely related** and often show up together.
Spanish and Portuguese are **closely related**, so speakers can often understand each other.

drill.sentence: The two break-ins are probably {{closely related}}; both happened on the same street on the same night.
drill.hint: have a lot to do with each other (adverb + participle; not *linked* or *connected*)

mistake.wrong: Dutch is closely related with German.
mistake.right: Dutch is closely related to German.
mistake.why: *Related* takes *to*; *with* is a common translation error.

entries.related: *distantly related* — the opposite for family; *interrelated* — connected in several ways; *unrelated* — not connected.

entries.label: prepositional phrase
entries.meaning: Containing or knowing the latest information.
entries.usage: Very common in speech, IT, news and office life. After a verb it has no hyphens (*keep your software up to date*, *stay up to date on the news*); before a noun it is hyphenated (*up-to-date information*). *Bring someone up to date* means to tell them the latest news.
entries.pattern: keep / stay up to date (on / with + noun); bring someone up to date; up-to-date + noun
examples: I keep my LinkedIn profile **up to date**, even when I'm not looking for a job.
I listen to the local news every morning to stay **up to date** on what's happening in town.
Can someone bring me **up to date** on what I missed while I was on vacation?

drill.sentence: Before you travel, check that your passport is valid and your contact details are {{up to date}}.
drill.hint: showing the latest information (three short words, no hyphens here)

entries.related: *current* — the one-word adjective; *out of date* — the opposite; *keep someone posted* — informal, keep giving them the latest news.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To collect money for a cause, project or business, for example through events, donations or investors.
entries.usage: Very common in charity, school and business contexts. Patterns are *raise money for* + cause and *raise money to* + verb; a *fundraiser* is the event, and *fundraising* is the activity. In business, *raise* alone often means to get investment: *They raised ten million dollars.*
entries.pattern: raise money for + cause / to + verb
examples: The kids sold lemonade all weekend to **raise money** for the animal shelter.
Our neighborhood association is **raising money** to plant trees along Main Street.
The two founders **raised money** from friends and family to open their first coffee shop.

drill.sentence: Every spring, the high school band holds a car wash to {{raise money}} for its trip to the state competition.
drill.hint: get people to donate (the verb is not *collect* or *make*)

entries.related: *fundraising* — the activity; *crowdfund* — raise money online from many people; *donate* — give money to a cause.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: A fast, easy solution that deals with a problem only for a short time or only on the surface.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, news and advice, and often negative: *There's no quick fix for back pain.* Patterns are *a quick fix for* + problem and *there's no quick fix*. It can be neutral when a temporary repair is all you need.
entries.pattern: a quick fix for + problem; there's no quick fix
examples: Duct tape is **a quick fix** for the broken side mirror, but I'll need a new one before winter.
Crash diets promise **a quick fix**, but the weight usually comes back.
Hiring temporary staff is just **a quick fix**; the hospital needs to keep the nurses it already has.

drill.sentence: There's no {{quick fix}} for learning a language; you just have to practice a little every day.
drill.hint: a fast, easy solution (adjective + noun; not *magic bullet* or *shortcut*)

entries.related: *a Band-Aid solution* — a temporary fix that hides the problem; *a stopgap* — a temporary measure; *a long-term solution* — the opposite.

entries.label: verb phrase
entries.meaning: To stop working for a period, for example for a vacation, an illness or family reasons.
entries.usage: Very common at work and in conversation. Patterns are *take time off (work)*, *take a day / a week off* and *take time off to* + verb. Americans also say *take vacation* or use *PTO* (paid time off), while British speakers *take holiday*.
entries.pattern: take (some) time off (work) (to + verb); take a day / a week off
examples: My husband **took time off** work to help out when the baby was born.
I haven't **taken** any **time off** since March, and I'm exhausted.
Small business owners often find it hard to **take time off** because no one can cover for them.

drill.sentence: She's {{taking time off}} from her job to travel around South America for three months.
drill.hint: stopping work for a while (not *leave* or *a break*)

mistake.wrong: I need to take a time off next week.
mistake.right: I need to take some time off next week.
mistake.why: *Time off* is uncountable, so use *some* or no article, not *a*.

entries.related: *take a break* — stop for a short time; *take leave* — formal, official time off; *call in sick* — tell work you're ill and won't come.

entries.label: prepositional phrase
entries.meaning: Already set up and working or in force, used of rules, systems, plans and procedures.
entries.usage: Common in business, government, safety and news. Patterns are *be in place*, *put something in place* and *have something in place*; typical subjects are rules, laws, policies, measures, systems and plans. It often appears with a time: *The new system will be in place by June.*
entries.pattern: be / put + noun + in place; have + noun + in place
examples: The new parking rules will be **in place** by the start of the school year.
Do you have a plan **in place** in case one of you loses your job?
Strict safety measures were **in place** at the stadium after last year's crowd problems.

drill.sentence: The building manager says a new security system is now {{in place}}, so the garage door locks automatically at night.
drill.hint: already working (a two-word prepositional phrase)

entries.related: *in effect / in force* — legally valid now, for laws and rules; *up and running* — informal, working; *set up* — create or arrange.

entries.label: verb phrase
entries.meaning: To decide to treat something as more important than other things and give it time or money first.
entries.usage: Common in speech and writing about health, family, work and public spending. The object goes in the middle (*make your health a priority*), or use *make it a priority to* + verb. *Top* often strengthens it: *make it a top priority*.
entries.pattern: make + noun + a priority; make it a priority to + verb
examples: After my heart scare, I **made** exercise **a priority**.
We **make it a priority** to eat dinner together as a family at least four nights a week.
The town has **made** fixing the roads **a priority** this year.

drill.sentence: She {{makes it a priority}} to call her grandmother every Sunday, no matter how busy she is.
drill.hint: treats it as more important than other things (the noun is not *point*)

entries.related: *prioritize* — the one-word verb; *put something first* — plainer; *make a point of* + *-ing* — make sure you do something deliberately.

entries.label: noun phrase
entries.meaning: A moment when a situation starts to change in an important and lasting way.
entries.usage: Common in stories about lives, careers, history, sports and illness. Patterns are *a turning point in* + noun (*a turning point in my life*) and *mark a turning point*. *The turning point* refers to the single decisive moment, for example in a game.
entries.pattern: a turning point in + life / career / history; mark a turning point
examples: Losing my job was **a turning point**; it pushed me to start my own business.
That second-half goal was **the turning point** of the game.
Historians see the printing press as **a turning point** in European history.

drill.sentence: Spending a summer with a host family in Mexico was {{a turning point}}; it's why she became a Spanish teacher.
drill.hint: a moment that changed the direction of her life (not *a milestone* or *a defining moment*)

entries.related: *a milestone* — an important stage reached, not necessarily a change; *a watershed moment* — a formal word for a major turning point; *a game changer* — informal, something that changes a situation completely.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To try hard to make someone do something, for example by persuading, demanding or threatening.
entries.usage: Common in news, business, sports and family life. The pattern is *put pressure on* someone *to* + verb, often with *a lot of*, *huge* or *increasing*. *Put pressure on yourself* means to expect too much of yourself, and *exert pressure on* is a more formal variant.
entries.pattern: put (a lot of) pressure on + someone (to + verb)
examples: My parents never **put pressure on** me to become a doctor or a lawyer.
Fans are **putting pressure on** the team's owner to fire the coach.
The salesman kept **putting pressure on** us to sign the contract that day.

drill.sentence: Her teammates were {{putting pressure on}} her to skip practice and go to the beach.
drill.hint: trying hard to make (not *pushing*)

entries.related: *pressure someone into* + *-ing* — force them by pressure; *lean on* — informal, pressure someone; *twist someone's arm* — informal, persuade someone who is unwilling.

entries.label: prepositional phrase
entries.meaning: Supporting or agreeing with a plan, idea or person.
entries.usage: Common in meetings, votes, debates and polls: *Who's in favor?* Patterns are *be in favor of* + noun or *-ing* and *vote in favor of* something; the American spelling is *favor*. *In favor of* can also mean choosing one thing instead of another: *They dropped the plan in favor of a cheaper one.*
entries.pattern: be / vote in favor of + noun / -ing
examples: Most parents in the survey were **in favor of** a later start time for high school.
The board voted seven to two **in favor of** building a new gym.
I'm all **in favor of** eating out tonight; I don't feel like cooking.

drill.sentence: When my sister suggested renting a cabin for Mom's sixtieth birthday, everyone was {{in favor of}} the idea.
drill.hint: supporting (a prepositional phrase ending in *of*; not *supportive of*)

entries.related: *for* — casual: *I'm all for it*; *in support of* — more formal; *against* / *opposed to* — the opposite.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To look directly into another person's eyes while they look into yours.
entries.usage: Common in talk about communication, job interviews, dating and parenting. The verb is *make*, with no article: *make eye contact with* someone; *avoid eye contact* and *hold eye contact* are also frequent. In American culture, steady eye contact usually signals honesty and confidence.
entries.pattern: make eye contact (with + someone); avoid / hold eye contact
examples: When you give a toast, **make eye contact** with a few guests instead of reading from your phone.
Our dog refuses to **make eye contact** whenever he's done something wrong.
In the elevator, everyone stared at their phones to avoid **making eye contact**.

drill.sentence: During an interview, {{make eye contact}} with whoever is asking the question instead of looking down at your notes.
drill.hint: look the person directly in the eyes (verb + two nouns; the verb is not *keep* or *maintain*)

mistake.wrong: Try to make an eye contact with the interviewer.
mistake.right: Try to make eye contact with the interviewer.
mistake.why: *Eye contact* is uncountable, so it takes no *a* or *an*.

entries.related: *look someone in the eye* — look straight at them, often to show honesty; *avoid eye contact* — the opposite; *stare* — look too long, which can seem rude.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: A worry that is reasonable and justified, so it should be taken seriously.
entries.usage: Common in meetings, news, customer service and polite disagreement: *That's a legitimate concern, and we're looking into it.* Typical patterns are *have legitimate concerns about* + noun and *address legitimate concerns*. *Legitimate* here means "reasonable", not "legal".
entries.pattern: have / raise a legitimate concern (about + noun)
examples: Parents have **a legitimate concern** about how much time their kids spend on screens.
Your worry about the cost is **a legitimate concern**, so let's look at cheaper options.
Neighbors pointed out **a legitimate concern**: the new building has only twenty parking spaces for eighty apartments.

drill.sentence: Whether the narrow road can handle all the extra traffic is {{a legitimate concern}}, not just an excuse to block the new stadium.
drill.hint: a justified worry (the adjective is not *valid*, *real* or *reasonable*)

entries.related: *a valid concern* — very similar; *a real concern* — plainer; *an unfounded fear* — a worry with no good reason.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To give up things you value, such as time, money or comfort, in order to achieve something more important.
entries.usage: Common when talking about parents, careers, athletes and long-term goals, and often used to express gratitude or respect: *My parents made a lot of sacrifices for us.* Patterns are *make sacrifices for* + person or goal and *make sacrifices to* + verb.
entries.pattern: make (a lot of / many) sacrifices for + person / goal
examples: My parents **made** huge **sacrifices** so that my sister and I could go to college.
To save for a house, we **made** some **sacrifices**: no vacations and no eating out for two years.
Olympic athletes **make sacrifices** most teenagers can't imagine, like training before school every day.

drill.sentence: Starting a business means {{making sacrifices}}; I haven't had a full weekend off in a year.
drill.hint: giving up things you care about (verb + plural noun)

mistake.wrong: She brought many sacrifices for her career.
mistake.right: She made many sacrifices for her career.
mistake.why: In English you *make* sacrifices; *bring sacrifices* is a word-for-word translation of German *Opfer bringen*.

entries.related: *give up* — stop having or doing something; *go without* — live without something you want; *pay the price* — suffer a cost because of a choice.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To make people think well of you, especially when they meet you for the first time.
entries.usage: Very common in talk about job interviews, dates, meeting a partner's family and first days at work. Patterns are *make a good impression on* + someone and *make a good first impression*; the opposite is *make a bad impression*.
entries.pattern: make a good (first) impression on + someone
examples: I wore my best suit to the interview because I really wanted to **make a good impression**.
He brought flowers for my mother and **made a good impression** on the whole family.
Clean bathrooms **make a good impression** on customers, even if they never mention it.

drill.sentence: It's my first day at the new job, so I want to {{make a good impression}} on my boss.
drill.hint: be seen positively from the start (the verb is not *leave*)

entries.related: *make a good first impression* — at the very first meeting; *leave a good impression* — be remembered well after you go; *impress* — the one-word verb.

entries.label: adjective + preposition
entries.meaning: To meet the official conditions to receive something, such as a benefit or a discount, or to take part in something.
entries.usage: Common in official letters, forms, HR, schools and government services. Patterns are *be eligible for* + noun and *be eligible to* + verb (*eligible to vote*); *ineligible* is the opposite, and *eligibility* is the noun. In casual speech, *qualify for* is often used instead.
entries.pattern: be eligible for + noun; be eligible to + verb
examples: Students under twenty-five **are eligible for** a discount on the monthly bus pass.
You'll **be eligible for** health insurance after ninety days with the company.
Kids who live within a mile of the school **aren't eligible for** the bus.

drill.sentence: If your income is below a certain level, you may {{be eligible for}} help with your heating bill.
drill.hint: meet the conditions to get (not *qualify for*)

entries.related: *qualify for* — same, more casual; *entitled to* — having a right to something; *ineligible* — not eligible.

entries.term: take a closer look at something
entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To examine something more carefully, often because the first look was not enough.
entries.usage: Very common in speech, news, teaching and reports, often to introduce detail: *Let's take a closer look at the numbers.* The pattern is *take a closer look at* + noun; *have a closer look* is more British. A closer look often reveals a problem.
entries.pattern: take a closer look at + noun
examples: The ring looked real, but when I **took a closer look**, I saw the stone was plastic.
Before you sign the lease, **take a closer look at** the fees in the small print.
In tonight's episode, we **take a closer look at** why grocery prices keep going up.

drill.sentence: The mechanic said the engine was fine, but he'd {{take a closer look}} at the brakes on Monday.
drill.hint: examine more carefully (the verb is not *have*)

entries.related: *take a look at* — examine quickly, more casual; *look into* — investigate; *scrutinize* — formal, examine very carefully.

entries.label: verb + adjective
entries.meaning: To keep your attention on your goal or task and not let other things distract you.
entries.usage: Very common in sports, school, work and self-help talk, and often said as encouragement: *Stay focused!* Patterns are *stay focused on* + noun or *-ing* and *stay focused* alone. *Remain focused* is a more formal variant.
entries.pattern: stay focused (on + noun / -ing)
examples: It's hard to **stay focused** in an open office with phones ringing all day.
The coach kept telling the players to **stay focused** on defense, even with a big lead.
I put my phone in another room so I can **stay focused** while I study for the bar exam.

drill.sentence: With the TV on and the kids running around, I find it impossible to {{stay focused}} on my tax forms.
drill.hint: not let anything distract me (the verb is not *remain* or *keep*)

entries.related: *concentrate* — the one-word verb; *keep your eye on the ball* — idiom, stay focused on what matters; *get distracted* — the opposite.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To have the right or chance to give your opinion and influence a decision.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, workplaces, local politics and family life, often in complaints: *We had no say in it.* Patterns are *have a say in* + noun and *have no / little / more say in* something. *Have the final say* means to make the final decision.
entries.pattern: have a / no / some say in + noun
examples: Teenagers should **have a say in** where the family goes on vacation.
Employees **had no say in** the decision to move the office to the suburbs.
Residents want to **have a say in** how the new park is designed.

drill.sentence: It's my house too, so I think I should {{have a say in}} what color we paint the living room.
drill.hint: be able to influence (the verb is not *get*)

entries.related: *have input into* — give opinions, more businesslike; *have the final say* — make the last decision; *have a voice in* — similar, more formal.

entries.label: prepositional phrase
entries.meaning: Intentionally; because you wanted to, not by accident.
entries.usage: Very common in speech, especially in accusations and denials: *You did that on purpose!* It usually comes at the end of the clause, after the verb and its object. *Deliberately* is more formal, and *by accident* is the opposite.
entries.pattern: do something on purpose
examples: My little brother spilled juice on my homework, and I'm sure he did it **on purpose**.
The architect made the windows small **on purpose** to keep the house cool in summer.
Sorry I stepped on your foot; it wasn't **on purpose**.

drill.sentence: The waiter forgot our drinks twice, but I don't think he did it {{on purpose}}.
drill.hint: intentionally (two words)

mistake.wrong: I'm sure she broke it by purpose.
mistake.right: I'm sure she broke it on purpose.
mistake.why: Learners say *by purpose* by analogy with *by accident*, but the fixed phrase is *on purpose*.

entries.related: *deliberately* — more formal; *intentionally* — neutral, often legal; *by accident* — the opposite.

entries.term: take the time to do something
entries.label: verb phrase
entries.meaning: To do something carefully or kindly even though you are busy, giving it the time it needs.
entries.usage: Common in thanks, advice and praise: *Thank you for taking the time to reply.* The pattern is *take the time to* + verb; *take time to* without *the* is also common. It is very frequent in polite emails and customer service.
entries.pattern: take the time to + verb
examples: Thank you for **taking the time to** meet with me; I know your schedule is packed.
Our pediatrician always **takes the time to** answer every question, even when the waiting room is full.
If you **take the time to** read the instructions, the bookcase is actually easy to put together.

drill.sentence: My neighbor {{took the time to}} show me how to fix the leaky faucet instead of just doing it herself.
drill.hint: patiently made the effort to (not *bothered to*)

entries.related: *make time for* — arrange your schedule to fit something in; *bother to* — make the effort, often in negatives; *take your time* — don't hurry.

entries.label: adverb + verb
entries.meaning: To be completely sure that something is true or right.
entries.usage: Common in speeches, interviews, opinion pieces and serious conversation; it sounds stronger and more formal than *really think*. Patterns are *firmly believe (that)* + clause and *firmly believe in* + noun or *-ing*. *Strongly believe* is also very common and means almost the same.
entries.pattern: firmly believe (that) …; firmly believe in + noun / -ing
examples: I **firmly believe** that every child should learn to swim.
My mother **firmly believes** in writing thank-you notes by hand.
Her lawyer **firmly believes** the case will be dismissed.

drill.sentence: My father-in-law {{firmly believes}} that a bowl of chicken soup can cure almost anything.
drill.hint: is completely sure (the adverb is not *strongly* or *truly*)

entries.related: *strongly believe* — almost the same; *be convinced* — certain after thinking or seeing evidence; *have doubts* — the opposite.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To accept or claim praise for something, often when you don't fully deserve it.
entries.usage: Common at work, in sports and in family life; it is usually critical when someone else did the work: *He took credit for my idea.* Patterns are *take credit for* + noun or *-ing* and *take (all) the credit*. *Give someone credit* is the opposite: praise the right person.
entries.pattern: take (the) credit for + noun / -ing
examples: My coworker **took credit for** the report even though I did most of the work.
I can't **take credit for** the cake; my daughter baked it.
The new CEO quickly **took credit for** a turnaround that had started before she arrived.

drill.sentence: He {{took credit for}} the garden, but his wife did all the planting and weeding.
drill.hint: accepted praise for (the verb is not *claimed*)

entries.related: *claim credit for* — similar, more active; *give credit where credit is due* — praise the right person; *steal the spotlight* — take attention away from others.

entries.label: prepositional phrase
entries.meaning: Later than the time that was planned.
entries.usage: Common at work, in construction, transportation and news. Patterns are *be / run / fall behind schedule*, often with a time: *two weeks behind schedule*, *way behind schedule*. The opposites are *on schedule* and *ahead of schedule*.
entries.pattern: be / run / fall (two weeks) behind schedule
examples: The new subway line is three years **behind schedule** and way over budget.
Our flight was running an hour **behind schedule**, so we got dinner at the airport.
We've fallen **behind schedule** with the baby's room; the crib still isn't put together.

drill.sentence: The renovation of our kitchen is three weeks {{behind schedule}} because the cabinets arrived late.
drill.hint: later than the plan (preposition + noun)

mistake.wrong: The project is two months behind the schedule.
mistake.right: The project is two months behind schedule.
mistake.why: In this fixed phrase *schedule* has no article.

entries.related: *ahead of schedule* — earlier than planned; *on schedule* — on time; *running late* — informal, behind for a short time.

entries.label: verb phrase
entries.meaning: To be the first thing you think of, or to appear in your thoughts when you think about a topic.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation, interviews and writing: *Nothing comes to mind.* The thing you think of is the subject (*A few names come to mind*), not the person who thinks. *Spring to mind* is a more vivid variant, and *the first thing that comes to mind* is a frequent frame.
entries.pattern: something comes to mind; the first thing that comes to mind
examples: When I think of summer, the smell of sunscreen and grilled corn **comes to mind**.
"Any good restaurants around here?" "Nothing **comes to mind**, but I'll ask my sister."
The word that **comes to mind** when I think of my first boss is patience.

drill.sentence: When you hear the words "Italian food," what's the first dish that {{comes to mind}}?
drill.hint: appears in your thoughts (the verb is not *springs*)

entries.related: *spring to mind* — come to mind quickly or vividly; *occur to someone* — a thought appears suddenly; *ring a bell* — seem familiar.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: Something that almost everyone, or everyone in a particular group, already knows.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, news and writing, usually as *It's common knowledge that* + clause or *X is common knowledge*. It takes no article. In academic writing, *common knowledge* also means facts that need no citation.
entries.pattern: it's common knowledge that …; X is common knowledge (among + group)
examples: It's **common knowledge** in our office that the coffee machine on the third floor is the good one.
Their engagement was **common knowledge** long before they made it official.
Today it's **common knowledge** that smoking causes cancer, but in the 1950s many doctors smoked.

drill.sentence: Everyone on the team knows it; it's {{common knowledge}} that the coach's son gets more playing time.
drill.hint: something everybody already knows (not *no secret*, *an open secret* or *well known*)

entries.related: *an open secret* — supposed to be secret, but known by everyone; *well known* — known by many people; *general knowledge* — broad facts, like those in a quiz.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To be willing to consider new ideas or other opinions before you form a judgment.
entries.usage: Common in advice and in conversations about food, travel, people and new plans: *Try to keep an open mind.* The pattern is *keep an open mind about* + noun; *open-minded* is the adjective. It often signals that the speaker expects some resistance.
entries.pattern: keep an open mind (about + noun)
examples: I didn't think I'd like sushi, but I **kept an open mind** and loved it.
The jury was told to **keep an open mind** until they had heard all the evidence.
When your kids bring home friends you're not sure about, try to **keep an open mind**.

drill.sentence: The new manager's ideas sound strange, but let's {{keep an open mind}} until we see the results.
drill.hint: stay willing to consider them (not *reserve judgment*)

entries.related: *open-minded* — the adjective; *reserve judgment* — wait before deciding; *narrow-minded* — the opposite, unwilling to accept new ideas.

entries.label: adverb + adjective
entries.meaning: Quite possible; something could easily happen or be true.
entries.usage: Common in speech and careful writing to admit a real possibility: *It's entirely possible that I'm wrong.* The usual pattern is *it's entirely possible (that)* + clause. It is stronger than *possible* alone, but it still doesn't mean *likely*.
entries.pattern: it's entirely possible (that) + clause
examples: It's **entirely possible** that I left my keys at the gym.
A late frost is **entirely possible** in April, so don't plant the tomatoes yet.
The doctor said it's **entirely possible** to live a normal life with this condition.

drill.sentence: I don't think he's angry; it's {{entirely possible}} he just didn't see your message.
drill.hint: really could be true (the adverb is not *quite*, *very*, *totally* or *perfectly*)

entries.related: *quite possible* — similar; *highly likely* — probable, not just possible; *out of the question* — not possible at all.

entries.label: verb phrase
entries.meaning: To believe that something is true, often when it turns out to be wrong.
entries.usage: Very common in polite conversation and emails, especially to correct a misunderstanding gently: *I was under the impression that the meeting was at ten.* It is usually in the past and often followed by a correction. It sounds softer and more polite than *I thought*.
entries.pattern: be under the impression (that) + clause
examples: I **was under the impression** that breakfast was included in the room price.
Sorry, we **were under the impression** you were vegetarian, so we made pasta.
Many people **are under the impression** that you need perfect credit to buy a house.

drill.sentence: My husband {{was under the impression}} that his sister was bringing dessert, so now we have none.
drill.hint: mistakenly believed (a polite phrase: *was* + preposition + noun)

entries.related: *get the impression* — start to feel something is true from what you see; *assume* — believe without proof; *be mistaken* — be wrong.

entries.term: have a tendency to do something
entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To often behave or happen in a particular way, as a habit or pattern rather than a single event.
entries.usage: Common in speech and writing, often to describe a small fault politely: *He has a tendency to interrupt.* The pattern is *have a tendency to* + verb; adjectives such as *natural* or *slight* can go before *tendency*. *Tend to* + verb is the shorter, more common form.
entries.pattern: have a (slight / natural) tendency to + verb
examples: My car **has a tendency to** pull to the left when I brake.
Like many first-time parents, we **had a tendency to** panic over every sneeze.
This part of the river **has a tendency to** flood after heavy spring rain.

drill.sentence: My brother {{has a tendency to}} exaggerate, so don't believe everything he tells you about his trip.
drill.hint: often does this (not *tends to*)

entries.related: *tend to* — the shorter, more common verb; *be prone to* — likely to suffer from or do something bad; *be inclined to* — likely to do or feel like doing.
